list.listitem: Acute epicondylitis can be managed with icing, relative rest, stretching, and eccentric strengthening exercises.B
NSAIDs are effective for acute tendonitis, but have no effect on long-term outcomes.B

Steroid injections are low risk, effective for short-term relief, and provide a relatively good long-term outcome potential. However, long-term results appear to be worse than with placebo injection.B

Physical therapy modalities, including eccentric strengthening, stretching, ultrasound, iontophoresis with NSAIDs, electrophysiotherapy, and bracing are safe, improve patient satisfaction, and may improve outcomes.B
Surgery has variable success rates and should only be considered after 6 months to 12 months of conservative therapy including steroid injections.B

background.definition: Medial or lateral epicondylitis is pain over the medial or lateral epicondyle that results from tendinopathy of the proximal insertion of the extensor or flexor tendons of the forearm due to repetitive or overuse trauma to the forearm.

list.listitem: The incidence of medial or lateral epicondylitis is 4 to 7 per 1000 patients per year in general practice.
Lateral epicondylitis 10 times more common than medial epicondylitis.
The prevalence of medial or lateral epicondylitis is 1% to 3% in overall population.

Mean total costs per patient with lateral epicondylitis treated with corticosteroid injections are approximately $600, compared with more than $800 per patient treated with a wait-and-see policy, and $1200 per patient for physical therapy.
A comparison of cost-utility ratios favored the wait-and-see approach.
Overuse injuries account for 7% of all injury-related physician office visits in the United States.
Medial and lateral epicondylitis are caused by any activity that produces a sudden load strain of the flexor or extensor compartment group or repetitive flexion or extension activity of the wrist.
Medial epicondylitis is caused by an initial insult to the wrist flexor muscle group, often followed by repetitive trauma to the inflamed tendons.
Lateral epicondylitis is caused by actions that involve forceful gripping and external rotation of the wrist.
See the table below for a list of risk factors.
The tendinous insertion of the forearm muscle groups is hypovascular and does not heal rapidly following an injury.

If the tendons are repetitively injured by a recreational activity such as tennis (lateral epicondylitis) or golf (medial epicondylitis) the inflammation will progress and potentially produce degenerative histologic changes.
In chronic injury, acute inflammatory changes are replaced by disordered collagen formation, increased proteoglycan ground substance, and neovascularization.

As chronic tendinopathy is no longer truly an inflammatory tendonitis, it does not respond to NSAIDs. This stage, which develops within 3 to 6 months of the onset of symptoms, is more accurately described as epicondylalgia or tendinosis.

The sympathetic nervous system (SNS) may contribute to tendinopathy, as it increases the innervation and abnormal catecholamine-producing tenocytes. The SNS activation of α-1 and α-2 adrenergic receptors, leading to the constriction or dilation of blood vessels, can affect the skin temperature around a pathological tendon.
Strengthening of grip and flexor or extensor groups can minimize the probability of developing epicondylitis.C
The primary culprit of "tennis elbow" is presumed to be a weak grip and poor backhand stroke, while "golfer's elbow" may be caused by overload in the swing that may be too steep or too flat.C
Using proper technique while participating in these activities may help prevent epicondylitis.C
Lateral epicondylitis pain is elicited with resisted wrist extension and supination while the elbow is in full extension.C
Medial epicondylitis pain is elicited with resisted wrist flexion and pronation.C
Focal tenderness over the epicondyle extending distally 1 cm to 2 cm along the tendon also suggests the diagnosis.C
MRI is more sensitive than ultrasound, but imaging should only be considered if the clinical diagnosis is in question.C

list.listitem: Patients typically present with elbow pain associated with activity. They may recall a single injury or describe a repetitive injury mechanism.
Palpation of the epicondyle out to 1 cm or 2 cm distal to the epicondyle elicits localized tenderness that replicates the pain experienced during activity.
Resisted flexion and supination of the forearm reproduces the pain of medial epicondylitis.
Extension of the arm with resisted extension of the wrist reproduces the pain of lateral epicondylitis.
Counterforce pressure applied distal to the point of maximal tenderness during flexion or extension decreases the point tenderness.
Ultrasound is specific but not as sensitive as MRI for detecting epicondylitis.
Radiographs may occasionally demonstrate calcification at the epicondyle or in the tendon but are not routinely recommended unless pain persists.
In general, order imaging studies only if the diagnosis is in question or after failure of 3 months to 6 months of conservative treatment.

One meta-analysis demonstrated that infrared thermography (a non-radiant technique) can be used to evaluate the temperature changes caused by tendinopathy in lateral epicondylitis (sensitivity 93%, specificity 97%, LR+ 31, LR- 0.07 although heterogeneity was noted).

Suspect epicondylitis in patients with pain elicited by resisted supination (lateral) or pronation (medical). Consider imaging (MRI or ultrasound) if the clinical diagnosis is in question or if the patient does not respond to initial conservative therapy.
Begin with relative rest with ice, NSAIDs, and stretching. If the patient desires a rapid return to work, consider a steroid injection (but still at least 2 weeks relative rest).

If symptoms persist, recommend physical therapy to strengthen the affected muscle group. If symptoms persist for 6 to 12 months, consider referral to an orthopedic surgeon, radiographic studies, and/or re-injection (maximum 3 per year).
Initial management of epicondylitis should include relative rest and icing.B
NSAIDs are effective in early management but there is insufficient evidence to support NSAIDs for chronic tendinosis.B
Steroid injections are low risk and are effective for short-term relief. However, more recent studies showed worse outcomes at one year with steroid injection.B
Physical therapy decreases pain and disability, provides excellent long-term recovery potential, and produces higher patient satisfaction.B
Topical or oral NSAID therapy is indicated for acute epicondylitis in the short term. However, there is insufficient evidence for or against the use of NSAIDs for chronic epicondylitis.
The effect of steroid injections is not entirely clear and depends on when the outcome was measured and what the steroid treatment was compared to.

For example, using a one year time frame a single injection of 10 mg of triamcinolone was associated with better outcomes (complete recovery or much improved) at 4 weeks (71% vs. 10%) but poorer outcomes (83% vs. 96%) at one year. However, the 4 week beneficial effect was no longer seen in the cohort with corticosteroid injection plus physiotherapy compared to saline plus physiotherapy.
Similarly, steroid injections show consistent benefit over NSAID therapy for acute epicondylitis at 4 weeks but not at 12 months.

In one RCT, a steroid injection had a 92% probability of short-term symptom resolution (compared with 47% for physical therapy and 32% for a wait-and-see policy). In a second RCT of 198 patients randomized to steroid injection, physical therapy, or conservative treatment, both steroid injection and PT were effective short-term, but there were more recurrences with injection and long-term outcomes were better with physical therapy.
Although most patients who receive a steroid injection achieve long-term success, higher long-term success rates are achieved with physical therapy or with a wait-and-see policy.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis showed no improvement in any outcomes with steriod injection, PRP injection, or botulinum toxin injection compared to placebo. A 2024 and a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing efficacy of PRP versus steroid injection for lateral epicondylitis both indicate that although short-term efficacy (1-2 months) is similar or may favor steroid injection, the 3-to-12-month efficacy favors PRP.

In a 2023 network meta-analysis, high-dose botulinum toxin (BoNT), low-dose BoNT, and corticosteroid injections were all effective compared to placebo in the reduction of pain at 2 to 6 weeks and 7 to 10 weeks after injection, but not at longer follow-up intervals. Contrary to prior meta-analyses, high-dose BoNT was more effective than low-dose, and low-dose more effective than corticosteroids, forpain reduction in the 2 to 6 and 7 to 10 week follow-up intervals. The re was lessbenefit tith longer follow-up. In evaluation of grip strength, high-dose BoNT and low-dose BoTN were more effective than corticosteroid in the short-term (2 to 6 weeks), but wot consistently swithlonger duration follow-up. High-dose BoTN had more adverse events compared to corticosteroid, with no difference between other groups. However, more studies are warranted to confirm these findings and further evaluate the dose-dependent effect of BoTN, and corticosteroid vs BoTN effectiveness and adverse events.

The most common procedure for recalcitrant lateral epicondylitis is exposure of and debridement of the extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle. Other common procedures for lateral epicondylitis are arthroscopic tenotomy, and percutaneous microtenotomy.
Surgery results in an 85% recovery to pretendonitis capability after excision of extensor carpi radialis brevis tendinosis.
A small RCT compared open with arthroscopic release in 37 patients with lateral epicondylitis and found no difference in outcomes.
Decompression of the posterior interosseous nerve versus lengthening of the extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle demonstrated a 50% success rate for lateral epicondylitis.

A randomized trial compared autologous conditioned plasma with low level laser therapy in patients with chronic lateral epicondylitis, and found no difference in outcomes. Given the uncertain value of low level laser, neither therapy can be endorsed based on this trial. NICE guidelines do not endorse this therapy as effective either.

A systematic review found that most patients treated with percutaneous microtenotomy using the microdebrider coblation wand had similar positive outcomes compared with the open or arthroscopic tenotomy techniques, with potentially lower rates of complication. However, a meta-analysis could not be performed due to heterogeneity of the methodology and small sample size.
Acupuncture may be effective for short-term pain relief in epicondylitis, but there have only been a few small studies.
Recommend absolute rest with avoidance of aggravating activities and progressive return to activity if required for job or recreation.

More than 40 different treatment methods have been described, but there is inconsistent evidence to support most modalities. In general, physical therapy decreases pain and disability and provides higher patient satisfaction.
Electrophysiotherapy and physical therapy improve pain scores and function compared to placebo.
Deep transverse friction massage as a treatment for lateral epicondylitis has been poorly studied (2 small RCTs), and those studies found no significant benefit.
Cryotherapy is indicated for relief of tendinopathy pain in acute tendonitis.
Eccentric strengthening is an effective treatment of tendonitis and may reverse degenerative changes and improve long-term recovery potential.
There was no clinically significant difference between the addition of an eccentric strengthening program and icing, stretching, and avoidance of aggravating factors.
Evidence is lacking to support the benefit of ultrasound or friction massage in treating epicondylitis.
Iontophoresis with steroids provides clinically insignificant benefit compared with placebo.

One review showed no clinically significant benefit from extracorporeal shock wave therapy (11 studies with 1104 patients.) This is consistent with prior studies.Another review indicated no improvement in overall pain, but found more patients reached 50% pain reduction at 3 months (9 studies with 715 patients).

Overall, there is insufficient evidence to support the use of orthotics. A small, methodologically weak randomized trial found no difference between wrist splints and forearm strap braces for patients with lateral epicondylitis.

There is significant interest in pro-inflammatory treatment modalities such as autologous blood injection (ABI) and platelet rich plasma (PRP) injection in the treatment of recalcitrant tendiopathies. A systematic review identified 7 RCTs with 515 patients comparing PRP with a steroid injection, and found a greater improvement in pain and function with PRP.

On the other hand, two subsequent systematic reviews found no benefit. A 2023 meta-analysis comparing PRP to placebo showed no significant difference between groups for pain control of lateral epicondylitis. They conclude that there is insufficient evidence to routinely recommend US guided PRP injections and to also consider the cost-benefit of this intervention.

A 2026 meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (5 double-blind) with 355 participants comparing PRP with saline or sham injection found no differences between groups in pain or function. Four of the studies were at low risk of bias and there was little heterogeneity.
Consider referral for physical therapy if the patient has the time to commit to a rehabilitation program.
Consider referral to an orthopedic surgeon if patient fails conservative therapy with 12 months of physical therapy and/or fails to improve after 2 steroid injections.
With conservative management and rest, approximately 85% of patients with epicondylitis are cured. Only half will recover at 1 year without treatment.B
Approximately 34% of patients presenting with complaint of elbow pain will still have pain in 1 year without treatment.B
Poorer outcomes are predicted for those with longer duration of the complaint at presentation and those with poor social support.B
